Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

---
title: "Quarterly Sales Report — Q2 2024"
subtitle: "Region: EMEA · internal, please do not forward"
author: "Analytics Team (prepared by M. Okafor)"
date: "`r format(Sys.Date(), '%d %B %Y')`"
output:

    toc_float:

      smooth_scroll: false
    number_sections: true
    df_print: paged
    code_folding: hide
    theme: flatly
    highlight: tango
params:
  region: "EMEA"
  quarter: 2
  fiscal_year: 2024
  fx_usd: 1.0813
editor_options:
  chunk_output_type: console
  markdown:
    wrap: sentence
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  fig.width = 9,
  fig.height = 5,
  fig.align = "center",
  dpi = 150
)

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
eur <- label_dollar(prefix = "€", big.mark = ",", accuracy = 1)
```

```{r load-data, cache=TRUE}
sales <- readr::read_csv(
  here::here("data", "sales_fy2024.csv"),
  col_types = readr::cols(order_date = readr::col_date("%Y-%m-%d"))
)
targets <- readxl::read_xlsx(here::here("data", "targets_fy24.xlsx"), sheet = "Q2")

q2 <- sales |>
  filter(region == params$region,
         lubridate::quarter(order_date) == params$quarter)

total_rev   <- sum(q2$net_revenue)
prev_rev    <- 11873420   # Q1 close, per Finance memo No. 3
growth_pct  <- (total_rev - prev_rev) / prev_rev
n_orders    <- nrow(q2)
n_customers <- n_distinct(q2$customer_id)
aov         <- total_rev / n_orders
```

<!-- MO 2024-07-09: numbers are from the 2024-07-08 extract. Re-knit after the July close
     in case Finance restates anything (they did last quarter, twice). -->


# Executive summary #

Net revenue for `r params$region` in Q`r params$quarter` `r params$fiscal_year` came to `r eur(total_rev)`, i.e. `r percent(growth_pct, accuracy = 0.1)` above Q1. This is the strongest quarter since the 2022 price change, although approx. one third of the uplift comes from two framework agreements signed in the last week of May.
Both deals were closed by Dr. Patel's team in Frankfurt; without them, growth would have been closer to 4% vs. the 6% we had planned.
The number of active customers rose to `r comma(n_customers)` (Q1: 1,412), while the average order value stayed roughly flat at `r eur(aov)`. For the group consolidation, which Acme Holdings Inc. reports in dollars to its U.S. shareholders, the headline figure is `r scales::dollar(total_rev * params$fx_usd)`; the unconverted amount, `r scales::dollar(total_rev)`, is what appears in the board pack with the € sign stripped (yes, really).

Three caveats up front.
First, April includes a one-off correction of €212k for invoices that were double-counted in March (see Finance memo No. 3 of 12 April).
Second, the UK entity migrated to the new ERP on 3 June at 4 p.m. CET, so a handful of orders
placed that evening were booked in early July.
We expect the effect to be small, but it is not zero!
Third, FX: all figures are converted at the monthly average rate published by Treasury, not at the transaction-date rate, which matters mostly for TRY and PLN (cf. the methodology note in the appendix).

> **TL;DR for the leadership call:** we beat the revenue target, mostly thanks to two deals that will not repeat in Q3. Margin is slightly below plan.
>
> The pipeline for Q3 looks _thin_ in the partner channel and __healthy__ in direct.
> See *Risks and next steps* before anyone commits to the H2 number.
>
> > Forwarded from the regional VP (11 July): "Please make sure the deck says clearly that the framework deals are one-offs. Last year the board extrapolated Q2 and we spent all of Q4 explaining why we missed."



# Revenue trend

```{r revenue-trend, fig.cap="Monthly revenue by channel, Q2 2024."}
q2 |>
  mutate(month = lubridate::floor_date(order_date, "month")) |>
  group_by(month, channel) |>
  summarise(revenue = sum(net_revenue), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(month, revenue, fill = channel)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 20) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = eur) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Net revenue", fill = "Channel")
```

Fig. 1 shows the usual pattern: April is soft, May is strong and June flattens out. Easter fell on 31 March this year, so the April dip is smaller than in 2023. Online grew in every single month.
The partner channel is lumpy, as always, because a handful of distributors place quarterly stocking orders; e.g. Brenntag-Nord alone accounted for €0.9m in May.
Direct sales were down 3% in June vs. May. That is within normal variation and we would not read much into it... but see the pipeline comments below.

Compared with Q2 2023 (Fig. 2 in last year's report), the mix has shifted towards online by roughly four percentage points.
Our working assumption, following Okafor et al. (internal analysis, 2023), is that about half of this shift is substitution from direct
rather than new demand. Nobody has tested that properly yet.

## Top products

```{r top-products, results='asis'}
top10 <- q2 |>
  group_by(sku, product_name) |>
  summarise(units = sum(quantity), revenue = sum(net_revenue), .groups = "drop") |>
  slice_max(revenue, n = 10)

kable(top10, format = "html", digits = 0,
      col.names = c("SKU", "Product", "Units", "Revenue (EUR)"),
      caption = "Top 10 products by net revenue, EMEA, Q2 2024") |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "condensed"), full_width = FALSE) |>
  print()
```

The 300-series still makes up six of the top ten. Hand-maintained KPI table below (Finance asked for exactly this format, sorry):

| KPI | Q2 actual | Target | Δ vs. target | Comment |
|:----|----------:|-------:|:------------:|:--------|
| Net revenue | `r eur(total_rev)` | €12.4m | +2.1 % | Includes the two framework deals; excluding them we are approx. 1.8 % *below* target |
| Orders | `r comma(n_orders)` |9,800| −4.0 % |Fewer, larger orders (partner channel) |
|Active customers| `r comma(n_customers)` | 1,450 | +3.2 % | Definition changed in April, see `customer_active_flag` in `finance_mart.dim_customer` |
| Gross margin | 41.7 % | 42.0 % | −0.3 pp | FX headwind (TRY, PLN); freight surcharges on the Rotterdam route |
| Returns rate| 2.9 % | ≤ 3.0 % | ok | |

## Regional breakdown {.tabset}

<!-- tabs only work in the HTML output; in the Word export the three sections simply follow each other -->

### EMEA

```{r region-emea, fig.height=4}
q2 |>
  count(country, wt = net_revenue, name = "revenue", sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 12) |>
  ggplot(aes(reorder(country, revenue), revenue)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2C7FB8") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = eur) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

Germany, France and the Netherlands account for 58% of EMEA revenue, up from 55% a year ago. Growth in the Nordics was driven by a single customer (Fjord Logistikk AS), so treat the +31% with care.
Southern Europe is flat.
Mr. Rossi's comment in the June forecast call ("Italy is waiting for the incentive scheme, nothing more.") still seems right to us. Société Lumière and Müller & Söhne GmbH both moved their orders from June into July.

### Americas

Shown for context only.
The Americas numbers are owned by the Austin team and are reported separately (their Q2 deck is linked at the bottom). Revenue was up 2.4% q/q.

### APAC

APAC had a weak quarter (−5.8% q/q). Most of the decline is Japan, where the yen lost approx. 7% vs. the euro over the quarter; in local currency Japan actually grew slightly.
Is this an FX story or a demand story? Mostly FX, we think.

- - -

# Channel mix and pipeline

The share of online revenue keeps creeping up, from 27% in Q2 2023 to 31% this quarter. A few observations, roughly in order of importance:

1. **Online.** Conversion improved after the checkout redesign went live on 22 April. Bounce rate on product pages fell from 48% to 41%, although part of that is a tracking change (the consent banner now loads asynchronously). We would like to see one more quarter before calling it structural.
2. **Partners.** Stocking orders are lumpy, e.g. two distributors ordered six months of stock in May.
   Two distributors in Poland have asked for extended payment terms (90 days vs. the usual 60). Finance has not decided yet.
3. **Direct.** Average deal size was €48k, about the same as in Q1. Win rate against our main competitor improved to 38% (Q1: 33%), which Sales attributes to the new bundle pricing; we have not been able to verify this independently.

The weighted pipeline for Q3 stands at €13.1m, i.e. approx. 1.05× the Q3 target. Historically we needed at least 1.2× coverage to hit the number, so this is tight.

* Pipeline by stage (weighted, € m):
  - Qualified: 4.2
  - Proposal: 5.0
      + of which deals > €250k: 2.1
      + of which renewals: 0.8
  - Negotiation: 3.9
* Slippage from Q2 into Q3: €1.4m across 23 opportunities.
    - Most of these are in DACH.
    - Three are flagged "customer budget freeze". One of them (opportunity No. 4471) has now been pushed four quarters in a row.

***

# Risks and next steps

Things that could move the Q3 number, as discussed with Prof. Lindqvist (our external advisor) on 4 July:

4) FX exposure in TRY, which is unhedged above €2m. A further 10% depreciation would cost us approx. €150k in reported revenue.
5) The ERP migration in France, currently planned for 2 September. If it slips, it slips into the busiest month of the quarter… not ideal.
6) The price increase on the 300-series (+4.5%, effective 1 August). Customers were notified in June. So far only two have objected in writing.

Next steps:

- [x] Share draft with the Regional VPs (done 9 July)
- [ ] Re-run after the July close and update the FX table
- [ ] Turn the Americas tab into a real comparison — currently just text
  - [ ] ask Austin for their extract (J. Álvarez)

========

Data notes
----------

The extract is taken from the `sales_fy2024` table in the warehouse (schema `finance_mart`), filtered to `region == "EMEA"` and `order_status %in% c("invoiced", "paid")`. title: "Chapter 3: Methods"
author: "Elena Vasquez-Hartmann"
date: "Draft — 18 April 2024"
output:
  bookdown::pdf_document2:
    toc: false
    number_sections: true
    keep_tex: true
    latex_engine: xelatex
    citation_package: biblatex

fontsize: 11pt
geometry: "margin=2.5cm"
header-includes:
  - \usepackage{booktabs}
  - \usepackage{siunitx}
  - \usepackage{float}
  - \floatplacement{figure}{htbp}
  - \sisetup{detect-all, per-mode = symbol}

```{r setup-ch3, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.pos = "htbp", out.extra = "")
library(tidyverse)
library(kableExtra)
library(lme4)

sites <- read_csv(here::here("data", "ch3", "sites.csv"),
                  show_col_types = FALSE)
```

# Methods {#methods}

<!-- EVH: section order follows the outline agreed with Dr. Brenner on
2024-02-27. The old 3.5 (pilot study) moved to Appendix B. -->

This chapter describes the study area, the field sampling design, the
laboratory procedures and the statistical models used to test the
hypotheses set out in Chapter \@ref(intro). Where a procedure follows a
published protocol closely I only summarise it and refer to the original
description [e.g., @biggs1996; @steinman2017, pp. 213--225]; any deviations are described in full.
All analyses were run in R [@R-base] with the packages listed in
Appendix \@ref(software).

## Study area {#study-area}

The study was carried out in twelve second- and third-order streams in
the upper Kinzig and Murg catchments of the northern Black Forest, SW
Germany (Figure \@ref(fig:study-area)). Both catchments are underlain by
Triassic sandstone (Buntsandstein) and granite. Mean annual
precipitation is ca. 1,600--1,900 mm and mean annual air temperature
approx. 7.5 °C at 800 m a.s.l. (DWD station No. 4927, 1991--2020
normals). Land use is dominated by managed spruce--fir forest;
agriculture is restricted to small pastures on the valley floors.

(ref:fig-study-area-cap) Location of the twelve study reaches in the upper Kinzig and Murg catchments (Black Forest, SW Germany). Open circles: shaded reaches; filled circles: open-canopy reaches. Basemap © OpenStreetMap contributors.

```{r study-area, fig.cap='(ref:fig-study-area-cap)', out.width='80%', fig.align='center'}
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("figures", "ch3", "study_area_map.pdf"))
```

Reaches were chosen from a pool of 31 candidate sites identified during
a reconnaissance survey in March 2021. The selection criteria were (i) a
wetted width of 2--6 m at base flow, (ii) no point-source inputs within
2 km upstream and (iii) safe access during high flows. Six reaches had a
closed riparian canopy (> 80 % cover, measured with a spherical
densiometer[^densiometer]) and six had been clear-cut or windthrown within the past
ten years, i.e. they were largely open (< 30 % cover). Paired reaches
were located in the same or in adjacent sub-catchments to minimise
differences in water chemistry, cf. @jones2018, who showed that
between-catchment variation in dissolved phosphorus can mask canopy
effects almost entirely.


## Sampling design {#sampling-design}

Each reach was visited on six occasions between April and September 2022
(Table \@ref(tab:sampling)). The field procedure was identical on every
visit:

1. On arrival, water temperature, conductivity and pH were recorded with
   a multiparameter probe (WTW Multi 3630 IDS, Xylem Inc., Weilheim) at
   the downstream end of the reach.
2. Five transects were laid out at equal distances along a 50 m reach.
   On each transect:
   - three cobbles (64--256 mm, *b*-axis) were selected at random
     positions using a random-number table, **not** by eye;
   - canopy cover was read with the densiometer facing upstream,
     downstream and towards both banks;
       * the four readings were averaged per transect;
       * on overcast days a second observer (Dr. Kowalski or the
         author) repeated the readings independently.
3. Periphyton was removed from a 4.9 cm² area on the upper surface of
   each cobble with a template and a stiff toothbrush, rinsed into a
   sample bottle with filtered stream water and made up to 50 mL. A
   \SI{5}{\milli\litre} aliquot was preserved in Lugol's solution for
   taxonomic analysis (not reported in this chapter, see Chapter 5).
4. Samples were kept dark and cool (ca. 4 °C) and filtered within 6 h
of collection.

```{r sampling}
tribble(
  ~Campaign, ~Dates,            ~Discharge, ~Notes,
  "C1",      "11--14 Apr 2022", "85--240",  "tail of snowmelt",
  "C2",      "16--19 May 2022", "40--130",  "",
  "C3",      "20--23 Jun 2022", "25--95",   "M4 repeated on 30 Jun (spate)",
  "C4",      "18--21 Jul 2022", "12--60",   "low flow; K3 and M2 partly dry",
  "C5",      "22--25 Aug 2022", "9--48",    "",
  "C6",      "19--22 Sep 2022", "30--110",  "leaf fall started at K2, K5"
) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE,
        col.names = c("Campaign", "Dates", "Discharge (L/s)", "Notes"),
        caption = "Sampling campaigns, dates and discharge range across reaches.") |>
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position", font_size = 9)
```

> **Field note, 23 June 2022 (reach M4).** Bed partly mobilised after
> the storm of 21 June; three of the five tiles were gone and the other
> two were buried under ca. 5 cm of sand. Campaign C3 for M4 was
therefore repeated a week later, on 30 June.

## Laboratory analyses

Chlorophyll *a* was extracted in 90 % ethanol at 75 °C for 5 min,
followed by 24 h in the dark at 4 °C, and measured spectrophotometrically
with correction for phaeopigments [@jespersen1978]. Ash-free dry mass
(AFDM) was determined by drying a second filter at 105 °C to constant
mass and combusting it at 500 °C for 4 h. Dissolved nutrients (SRP,
NO~3~-N, NH~4~-N) were analysed by the central laboratory of the
Institute (Dr. M. Schäfer) by continuous-flow analysis; detection limits
were 2 µg L^-1^ for SRP and 5 µg L^-1^ for both nitrogen species. Values
below the detection limit were set to half the limit. This affected 7 %
of the SRP measurements but none of the nitrate values.

## Periphyton growth model {#growth-model}

Accrual of chlorophyll *a* on artificial substrata (unglazed ceramic
tiles, 4.7 × 4.7 cm) deployed for 35 days was described by a logistic
model, following @biggs1996 and @stevenson1996 [-@stevenson1996]:

\begin{equation}
  B(t) = \frac{K}{1 + \left(\frac{K - B_0}{B_0}\right) e^{-r t}}
  (\#eq:growth)
\end{equation}

where $B(t)$ is chlorophyll *a* biomass (µg cm^-2^) at time $t$ (days
since deployment), $B_0$ the initial biomass, $K$ the carrying capacity
and $r$ the intrinsic growth rate (d^-1^). Equation \@ref(eq:growth) was
fitted separately for each reach and deployment by nonlinear least
squares (`nls()` with the port algorithm), constraining $K$ to be
positive. Following @doe2020 [p. 45], fits with fewer than five non-zero
observations were discarded; this removed 4 of 72 deployments (viz. K3
in C1, M4 in C3, and M2 and M6 in C4). Where the logistic model failed to converge,
a Gompertz model was fitted instead, cf. Eq. 2.4 in Chapter
\@ref(background); the two give nearly identical estimates of $r$ when
$B_0 \ll K$ [@smith2019; @doe2020, p. 45].

\newpage

## Statistical analysis {-}

Differences between shaded and open reaches were tested with linear
mixed-effects models of the form

$$
\log(y_{ijk}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{canopy}_i + \beta_2\,\text{campaign}_j + \beta_3\,(\text{canopy} \times \text{campaign})_{ij} + u_{\text{pair}} + u_{\text{reach}} + \varepsilon_{ijk}
$$

with random intercepts for reach pair and for reach nested in pair. The
response variables were (1) chlorophyll *a*, (2) AFDM, (3) the
autotrophic index (AFDM : chl *a*) and (4) the growth rate $r$ from
Eq. \@ref(eq:growth). Models were fitted by REML with **lme4**
[@bates2015]; *p*-values for the fixed effects were obtained with the
Kenward--Roger approximation. Model assumptions were checked visually
(residuals vs. fitted values, Q--Q plots), e.g. for heteroscedasticity
between campaigns. Where needed, a variance structure was added with
**nlme**, i.e. `varIdent(form = ~ 1 | campaign)`.

```{r model-example, eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE}
m_chla <- lmer(log(chla) ~ canopy * campaign + (1 | pair/reach),
               data = periphyton, REML = TRUE)
anova(m_chla, ddf = "Kenward-Roger")
```

Effect sizes are reported as back-transformed ratios with 95 %
confidence intervals. I did not correct for multiple testing across the
four response variables, since they are strongly correlated and
represent different facets of the same hypothesis [cf. @gelman2012];
this decision is revisited in the Discussion (Section
\@ref(disc-limits)). As @jones2018 put it, "the canopy effect is either
large enough to see in every metric, or it is not there at all."



***

## Open issues (remove before submission) {-}

- [ ] Densiometer footnote: cite the manufacturer's manual or Lemmon
    (1956)?

[^densiometer]: Model-C convex spherical densiometer (Forestry
    Suppliers Inc., Jackson, MS, U.S.A.). Readings were converted to
    percent cover following the manufacturer's instructions, i.e. by
    multiplying the number of covered points by 1.04.

    Lemmon's original description (1956) uses a slightly different
    grid; the difference is negligible for canopy cover above ca. 20 %.

---
title: "Getting started with tidyfoo"
author: "Priya Raman and Tomás Ferreira"
date: "`r Sys.Date()`"
output:
  rmarkdown::html_vignette:
    toc: true
    toc_depth: 2
vignette: >
  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Getting started with tidyfoo}
  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
editor_options:
  markdown:
    wrap: none
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

```{r setup}
library(tidyfoo)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
```

Survey platforms such as Qualtrics, LimeSurvey and SoSci Survey all export data in slightly different shapes: some put the question text in a second header row, some encode "don't know" as `-99`, others as `999` or as an empty string, and almost all of them produce column names like `Q12_3_TEXT` that mean nothing outside the original questionnaire. tidyfoo gives you a small set of verbs that turn such an export into a tidy data frame with one row per respondent, consistent column names, proper factors for Likert items and a codebook you can hand to your co-authors, i.e. the boring 80% of every survey project that nobody wants to write twice.

This vignette walks through a complete, if small, example. It assumes you know the basics of dplyr (e.g. `filter()`, `mutate()` and the pipe); if not, the [data transformation chapter of R for Data Science](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-transform.html#introduction) is a good place to start. Everything below runs in a few seconds on the example data that ships with the package, so feel free to copy the code into a script and follow along.

<!-- TODO (TF): add the speeders plot once the ggplot2 3.5 release is on CRAN; the current version needs the dev branch -->

## The example data

tidyfoo ships with a small, anonymised extract from a well-being survey run by Dr. Amara Okonkwo's group at the University of Leeds in 2023 (n = 412, 57 columns). The raw Qualtrics export is included as-is, warts and all, so that you can see exactly what each step does to it. Respondents gave informed consent for the anonymised data to be shared for teaching purposes; free-text answers were removed beforehand, as were IP addresses and the approx. location fields that Qualtrics adds by default.

```{r}
path <- tf_example("wellbeing_2023.csv")
raw <- tf_read(path, platform = "qualtrics")
dim(raw)
names(raw)[1:12]
```

`tf_read()` already does a few things for you: it drops the second and third header rows that Qualtrics adds (question text and import IDs), stores the question text as a `label` attribute on each column, and converts the `StartDate`/`EndDate` columns to `POSIXct` in the time zone recorded in the file. It does *not* rename anything or touch the values yet, because those decisions depend on your questionnaire and we would rather you made them explicitly.


## The verbs ##

The package is built around a handful of verbs that each do one thing:

- `tf_clean_names()` --- turns `Q12_3_TEXT` into something like `q12_3_text`, or, if you supply a lookup table, into a meaningful name such as `sleep_quality_text`.
- `tf_recode_missing()` --- converts platform-specific missing codes (`-99`, `-77`, `999`, `""`) to `NA`, optionally keeping the reason in a separate column.
- `tf_recode_likert()` --- turns item responses into ordered factors with consistent levels.
    - Works on labels ("Strongly agree") as well as on numeric codes.
    - Reverse-coded items are handled via `reverse = c(...)`; no more `6 - x` scattered across your scripts.
- `tf_score()` --- computes scale scores (mean or sum) with a minimum-valid-items rule.
- `tf_codebook()` --- produces a codebook as a data frame, or as HTML/Word via `tf_codebook_render()`.

* `tf_check()` --- runs a battery of plausibility checks (straight-lining, speeders, out-of-range values) and returns a tidy report.

Most verbs take a data frame as their first argument and return a data frame, so they compose with the pipe. The exceptions are `tf_labels()` and `tf_codebook()`, which return a tibble *describing* your data rather than the data itself.

## A typical workflow

In practice we nearly always go through the same steps, in this order:

1. Read the export with `tf_read()` and look at the labels (`tf_labels(raw)`).
1. Clean the names. For anything you will actually analyse, use a lookup table rather than the automatic names: the automatic names are fine for exploration, but they change whenever the questionnaire changes, e.g. when an item is added in a later wave or the platform renumbers the blocks.
1. Recode missing values.
1. Recode Likert items and compute scale scores.
1. Run `tf_check()` and decide, *before* looking at the outcomes, which respondents to exclude. Write that decision down (a pre-registration is ideal, a comment in the script is the bare minimum).
1. Write the codebook.

Steps 2--4 look like this:

```{r}
lookup <- tf_example_lookup("wellbeing_2023")
head(lookup, 4)

clean <- raw |>
  tf_clean_names(lookup = lookup) |>
  tf_recode_missing(codes = c(-99, -77)) |>
  tf_recode_likert(
    starts_with("wemwbs_"),
    levels = c("None of the time", "Rarely", "Some of the time", "Often", "All of the time")
  ) |>
  tf_score(wemwbs_total = starts_with("wemwbs_"), fun = "sum", min_valid = 12)

clean |>
  select(respondent_id, age_group, wemwbs_total) |>
  head()
```

The WEMWBS has 14 items scored 1--5, so totals range from 14 to 70; `min_valid = 12` means that a respondent needs at least 12 valid items for a total to be computed, and the remaining items are prorated.[^prorate] If you would rather not prorate, set `prorate = FALSE` and any respondent with a missing item gets `NA`. Which option is better depends on the instrument and on why the items are missing, cf. the discussion in Mazza et al. (2015) and the scoring guidance by Tennant et al. (2007), and we deliberately do not pick a default that hides the choice from you.

## Checking data quality

`tf_check()` never removes anything by itself. It flags, and you decide:

```{r}
report <- tf_check(clean, duration = "duration_sec", items = starts_with("wemwbs_"))
report
```

When a check cannot be run, you get an informative error rather than a silent `NA`:

```{r, error = TRUE}
tf_check(clean, duration = "time_taken")
```

| Check | Default threshold | Argument | Notes |
|:------|------------------:|:---------|:------|
| Speeders | < 1/3 of median duration | `speed_ratio` | Uses `duration_sec` unless you say otherwise |
| Straight-lining | ≥ 10 identical consecutive answers | `max_run` | Only within the item set you pass to `items` |
| Out of range | outside the declared levels | --- | Needs the Likert items recoded first |
|Duplicates|identical `ResponseId`, or IP + user agent|`dup_keys`|IP addresses are hashed by `tf_read()` by default|

## Codebooks

```{r, eval = FALSE}
tf_codebook(clean) |>
  tf_codebook_render("codebook.docx", title = "Well-being survey 2023 — codebook")
```

The rendered codebook lists every variable with its label, type, levels and the number of missing values. It looks roughly like this (truncated, and not evaluated here because the output is wide):

```r
tf_codebook(clean)
#> # A tibble: 41 × 6
#>   variable      label                                    type  n_missing levels
#>   <chr>         <chr>                                    <chr>     <int> <chr>
#> 1 respondent_id Response ID                              chr           0 NA
#> 2 age_group     What is your age?                        ord           3 18-24 | 25-34 | …
#> 3 wemwbs_01     I've been feeling optimistic about the…  ord           5 None of the time | …
#> # ℹ 38 more rows
```

> **Note:** the codebook uses the question text stored by `tf_read()`. If you created columns yourself, give them a label with `tf_label()` first, otherwise the label column will just say `NA`.
>
> Labels survive most dplyr verbs, but not all of them; `summarise()` drops them, for instance, and so does `pivot_longer()`.



***

Learn more
----------

- The [function reference][ref] lists every exported function, grouped by verb.
- `vignette("longitudinal", package = "tidyfoo")` shows how to stack several survey waves and keep the labels consistent across them, incl. waves that were fielded on different platforms (e.g. LimeSurvey in 2021 vs. Qualtrics from 2022 on).
- `vignette("lookup-tables")` explains the lookup format in detail, and how to version it alongside your questionnaire.
- Bugs and feature requests go to <https://github.com/tidyfoo/tidyfoo/issues>. Please include a small reprex, e.g. made with `reprex::reprex()`, and the output of `sessionInfo()`.

If you use tidyfoo in published work, please cite it; `citation("tidyfoo")` gives you the reference in BibTeX and plain text.\
Thanks to Dr. Okonkwo and her team for letting us ship their data, and to everyone who filed issues during the beta.

---
title: "Lab notebook — March 2024"
author: "Kenji Nakamura"
date: "Last knitted `r format(Sys.time(), '%Y-%m-%d %H:%M')`"
output:
  github_document:
    html_preview: false
    toc: true
    toc_depth: 2
editor_options:
  markdown:
    wrap: sentence
    canonical: true
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.path = "figs/2024-03/", dpi = 200)
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
gel  <- read_excel("data/2024-03-11_gel_densitometry.xlsx", sheet = "lanes")
brad <- read_csv("data/2024-03-13_bradford.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

Project: expression and purification of His~6~-tagged **PfkB-like kinase (construct pKN-17)** for the thermal-shift and crystallisation trials.\
Supervisor: Prof. Albrecht. Day-to-day questions: Dr. Nguyen.
Bench: room 2.14, shelf C. Freezer box "KN-2024-A".

<!-- Reminder to self: canonical: true means RStudio's visual editor rewrites this file on save. Don't panic about the diffs. -->

## 2024-03-04 (Mon)

Transformed pKN-17 into *E. coli* BL21(DE3) (NEB cat. No. C2527, lot 10183). Heat shock 30 s at 42 °C, recovery 1 h in SOC, plated on LB + kanamycin (50 µg/mL).
Also plated the empty-vector control and a no-DNA control.

Plan for the week, roughly:
1. Mon: transformation
2. Tue: overnight culture, then 1 L expression culture
3. Thu: lysis + Ni-NTA
4. Fri/Mon: SDS-PAGE, Bradford, decide whether to scale up

Ordered fresh imidazole (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, U.S.) because the old bottle is yellowish. Dr. Nguyen says it's fine for washing buffers but not for elution... I'm not convinced either way, so new bottle it is.
Also made 500 mL of 0.5 M EDTA stock, pH 8.0 (took forever to dissolve, as usual).

## 2024-03-05 (Tue)

Colonies! ca. 200 on the pKN-17 plate, none on the no-DNA control.
Picked 3 colonies into 5 mL LB + Kan, 37 °C, 220 rpm, in the morning. At 5 p.m. inoculated 1 L 2×YT (+ Kan) with 10 mL of the culture from colony No. 4, which had grown fastest.
OD~600~ readings:

| Time  | OD600 | Note |
|------:|:-----:|:-----|
| 17:00 | 0.08 | |
| 19:30 | 0.41 | |
| 20:15 | 0.68 | induced with 0.5 mM IPTG, moved to 18 °C |
| next day 09:00 | 3.9 | harvested, 4,000 × g, 20 min, 4 °C |

Induction at 18 °C overnight vs. 37 °C for 3 h: going with the cold induction because Kim et al. (2019) report that the protein is mostly insoluble at 37 °C. Their Fig. 2B is pretty convincing, although they used a different tag (GST) and a different strain.
Pellet stored at −80 °C.

## 2024-03-07 (Thu)

Lysis and Ni-NTA purification.
Pellet (approx. 6.2 g wet weight) resuspended in 40 mL lysis buffer, sonicated 6 × 30 s on ice, spun 30 min at 20,000 × g. Supernatant clear-ish; pellet large.

Buffers used:

| Buffer | Composition | pH | Volume |
|:--|:--|:-:|--:|
| Lysis | 50 mM Tris, 300 mM NaCl, 10 mM imidazole, 1 mM `TCEP`, protease inhibitor (1 tablet / 50 mL) | 8.0 | 50 mL |
| Wash | as lysis but 30 mM imidazole | 8.0 |100 mL|
|Elution| as lysis but 250 mM imidazole | 8.0 | 15 mL |
| Dialysis | 25 mM HEPES, 150 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM `TCEP`, 5 % glycerol | 7.5 | 2 × 2 L |

Steps (see [protocol P-07 v3][p07] on the shared drive for the details):

1. Bound supernatant to 2 mL Ni-NTA resin for 1 h at 4 °C on a rotator.
2. Washed with 3 × 10 CV wash buffer.
   The flow-through from the second wash was still slightly yellow. Is that the resin or the protein? Kept a sample.
3. Eluted in 5 × 1 mL fractions. Fractions E2--E4 were visibly cloudy at first, then cleared up after ca. 20 min on ice!
4. Pooled E2--E4 and dialysed overnight against dialysis buffer (2 × 2 L, one change at 11 p.m.).

Note: forgot to take a "total lysate" sample before spinning. I'll have to rely on the pellet sample for the solubility comparison. Not great, but not fatal either.

## 2024-03-11 (Mon)

SDS-PAGE (12 % Bis-Tris, MES buffer, 200 V, 35 min) of the lysate pellet, supernatant, flow-through, washes W1--W3 and elution fractions E1--E5. Strong band at the expected size (ca. 34 kDa) in E2--E4, i.e. in the soluble fraction.
Fainter band in the pellet.
Densitometry in ImageJ, background-subtracted (rolling ball, r = 50 px), three technical replicates per lane.

```{r gel-quant, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Band intensities. Error bars show s.d."}
gel |>
  group_by(lane_label) |>
  summarise(mean_int = mean(intensity), sd_int = sd(intensity), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(lane_label = fct_inorder(lane_label)) |>
  ggplot(aes(lane_label, mean_int)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey60") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_int - sd_int, ymax = mean_int + sd_int), width = 0.3) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Integrated intensity (a.u.)")
```

The band in E3 is approx. 4× the pellet band. Purity by densitometry ≈ 85 %, which is good enough for the thermal shift assay but not for crystallisation. (See Fig. 3 in the group-meeting slides for the comparison with last year's prep.)

***

## 2024-03-13 (Wed)

Bradford assay (BSA standards 0--1.0 mg/mL, triplicates, 595 nm).
Standard curve linear up to 0.8 mg/mL, R² = 0.996. The dialysed pool comes out at `r round(mean(brad$conc[brad$sample == "pool"]), 2)` mg/mL (mean of three dilutions), i.e. a total yield of roughly 9 mg from 1 L of culture.

Concentration estimates disagree between methods, as usual:

- Bradford: see above
- A280 (NanoDrop, ε = 27,960 M⁻¹ cm⁻¹ from [ProtParam][protparam]): 2.6 mg/mL
    - the 260/280 ratio is 0.71, so there is some nucleic acid contamination
    - Dr. Nguyen suggests a heparin column, or simply a higher-salt wash next time
- BCA: not done (kit expired in Feb.)

Which one to trust? For the TSA I'll go with A280, since the dye-binding assays tend to underestimate His-tagged proteins (e.g. Gomez et al. 2017, though their sample size was small).

## 2024-03-18 (Mon)

Meeting with Prof. Albrecht and Dr. Nguyen, 10--11 a.m.

> Prof. A.: "If the TSA shows a clean melt, don't bother with a second purification step yet. If it doesn't, we need SEC anyway."
>
> Agreed to run the TSA first. Dr. N. will order the SEC column (Superdex 75 Increase 10/300, approx. €3,100) regardless, since the group needs it for the other constructs too.

Also discussed the discrepancy with Kim et al. (2019).
They report K~m~ = 45 ± 6 µM for fructose-6-phosphate; our preliminary assay last month gave 120 µM, but at 25 °C vs. their 30 °C and in a different buffer. So not obviously a contradiction. Prof. A. thinks the difference is
the Mg²⁺ concentration (we use 2 mM, they use 10 mM).
Mr. Okoro pointed out that their enzyme was also a different isoform... which nobody had noticed.

## 2024-03-21 (Thu) ##

Thermal shift assay[^tsa], SYPRO Orange 5×, protein 5 µM, 20 µL per well, 25--95 °C at 1 °C/min on the QuantStudio.
Conditions: apo, + 1 mM ATP, + 1 mM ADP, + 5 mM F6P, + ATP/F6P. Clean single transitions in all wells.

* T~m~ (apo) = 47.8 ± 0.3 °C (n = 4)
* T~m~ (+ ATP) = 51.2 ± 0.2 °C, i.e. a shift of +3.4 °C
* T~m~ (+ ATP/F6P) = 53.9 ± 0.4 °C
  + significantly different from ATP alone (Welch's t-test, p < 0.05; n = 4 each, so take it with a grain of salt)
* ADP: no shift. F6P alone: +0.6 °C, probably not meaningful.

So the protein is folded and binds ATP. Good news!

Monthly summary
---------------

Copy-pasted to the group wiki, as usual.
The pKN-17 prep works. Yield ca. 9 mg/L, purity ≈ 85 %, and the TSA confirms ATP binding with a ΔT~m~ of +3.4 °C. The main issue is nucleic acid contamination (A260/280 = 0.71). The next prep will add a 1 M NaCl wash and a SEC step, i.e. the standard two-step protocol from Mr. Okoro's thesis.

### TODO

- [x] order new imidazole
- [x] TSA with ATP/ADP/F6P
- [ ] repeat prep with high-salt wash (week of 2024-04-01)
- [ ] SEC once the column arrives --- Dr. N. says "early April"
- [ ] kinetics at 30 °C, 10 mM Mg²⁺, to compare with Kim et al. (2019)
  - [ ] make fresh coupling enzymes (PK/LDH)
  - [ ] check whether the plate reader has its 340 nm filter back from service
- [ ] write up methods for the progress report (due **19 April**)


[^tsa]: Protocol adapted from Niesen et al. (2007), Nat. Protoc. 2: 2212--2221. Final DMSO concentration 1 %.

[p07]: https://drive.lab-albrecht.example/protocols/P-07_NiNTA_v3.pdf
[protparam]: https://web.expasy.org/protparam/ "ExPASy ProtParam"

---
title: "Interim Safety Summary: Study ACME-301"
subtitle: "Data cut-off 31 January 2024 — DSMB open session report"
author:
  - "Dr. A. Rivera, MD"
  - "B. Chen, PhD"
  - "S. O'Neill, MSc (Biostatistics)"
date: "`r format(Sys.Date(), '%d %B %Y')`"
output:
  word_document:
    reference_docx: template.docx
    toc: true
    toc_depth: 2
  pdf_document:
    latex_engine: xelatex
    toc: true
    number_sections: true
params:
  data_cut: "2024-01-31"
  arm_labels: ["Placebo", "Low dose", "High dose"]
  show_listings: false
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4, dpi = 300)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(haven)
library(knitr)

adsl <- read_sas("data/adam/adsl.sas7bdat") |>
  filter(SAFFL == "Y")
adae <- read_sas("data/adam/adae.sas7bdat") |>
  filter(TRTEMFL == "Y", ASTDT <= as.Date(params$data_cut))

adsl$TRT01A <- factor(adsl$TRT01A, levels = params$arm_labels)
adae <- adae |> left_join(select(adsl, USUBJID, TRT01A), by = "USUBJID")

n_randomized <- nrow(adsl)
pct_ae       <- 100 * n_distinct(adae$USUBJID) / n_randomized
n_sae        <- n_distinct(adae$USUBJID[adae$AESER == "Y"])
```

<!-- QC: checked by BC 2024-02-05 against the TLF shells v1.3. Two discrepancies in the AE table were traced to a MedDRA version mismatch (26.0 vs. 26.1) and fixed in ADAE. -->

# Purpose of this report

This report summarises the cumulative safety data from Study ACME-301, a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase II study of ACM-4410 in adults with moderate-to-severe chronic plaque psoriasis, for the open session of the Data Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) meeting on 21 February 2024. Data are presented by treatment arm, pooled across sites, i.e. without unblinding of individual participants. As agreed in the DSMB charter (v2.0, section 6.3), efficacy data are **not** included in the open report; see the [protocol][prot] and the [statistical analysis plan][sap] for definitions.

As of the data cut-off (`r params$data_cut`), `r n_randomized` participants had been randomised and had received at least one dose of study drug (safety population). Enrolment is approx. 68% complete vs. the planned 270 participants. Recruitment at the U.S. sites has been slower than projected, mainly because of competing studies, while the EU sites are on track. Dr. Rivera has asked the CRO to open two additional sites in Poland (site No. 314 and No. 315) in March.

# Study population

```{r demographics, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
demo <- adsl |>
  group_by(TRT01A) |>
  summarise(
    N = as.character(n()),
    `Age, mean (SD)` = sprintf("%.1f (%.1f)", mean(AGE), sd(AGE)),
    `Female, n (%)` = sprintf("%d (%.0f%%)", sum(SEX == "F"), 100 * mean(SEX == "F")),
    `BMI, mean (SD)` = sprintf("%.1f (%.1f)", mean(BMI), sd(BMI)),
    `PASI at baseline, median` = sprintf("%.1f", median(BASEPASI))
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(-TRT01A, names_to = "Characteristic") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = TRT01A, values_from = value)

knitr::kable(demo, align = "lccc",
             caption = "Table 1. Baseline demographics (safety population)")
```

Baseline characteristics were broadly balanced across arms (Table 1). The high-dose arm had a slightly higher proportion of participants with prior biologic exposure (31% vs. 24% on placebo), which is well within what one would expect by chance with arms of this size, cf. the simulations in the SAP, Appendix C.

# Exposure

Median duration of exposure was 16.1 weeks (range 2.0–24.0). Twelve participants discontinued study drug early:

- Placebo: 5 (lack of efficacy: 3; withdrawal of consent: 2)
- Low dose: 3
    - adverse event: 1 (SAE No. 2, see below)
    - lost to follow-up: 2
- High dose: 4
    * adverse event: 2
    * relocation: 1 — the participant moved abroad and could not attend visits
    * other: 1

# Adverse events #

Overall, `r sprintf("%.1f%%", pct_ae)` of participants experienced at least one treatment-emergent adverse event (TEAE). The most frequent TEAEs by MedDRA preferred term were nasopharyngitis, headache and upper respiratory tract infection, with no clear dose-response pattern (Fig. 1). Injection-site reactions were reported more often with active treatment (e.g., 9.8% in the high-dose arm vs. 2.2% on placebo), as expected from the phase I data reported by Lindgren et al.[^phase1] All injection-site reactions were grade 1 or 2 and none led to discontinuation.

```{r ae-plot, fig.cap="Fig. 1. Most frequent TEAEs (≥ 5% in any arm) by treatment arm."}
adae |>
  distinct(USUBJID, TRT01A, AEDECOD) |>
  count(TRT01A, AEDECOD) |>
  group_by(AEDECOD) |>
  filter(max(n) / n_randomized * 3 >= 0.05) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, reorder(AEDECOD, n), fill = TRT01A)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(x = "Participants", y = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

Grade ≥ 3 TEAEs (CTCAE v5.0) were infrequent:

| Category | Placebo | Low dose | High dose |
|:---------|:-------:|:--------:|:---------:|
| Any TEAE | 58 (64.4 %) | 61 (67.8 %) | 64 (71.1 %) |
| TEAE grade ≥ 3 | 3 (3.3 %) | 4 (4.4 %) |6 (6.7 %)|
|Serious AE (SAE)| 2 (2.2 %) | 2 (2.2 %) | 3 (3.3 %) |
| AE leading to discontinuation | 0 | 1 (1.1 %) | 2 (2.2 %) |
| Deaths | 0 | 0 | 0 |

_Note:_ the table above is hand-copied from TLF 14.3.1.1 (run of 2024-02-04); if it ever disagrees with the programmed output, the programmed output takes precedence.

## Serious adverse events

There were `r n_sae` participants with SAEs as of the data cut. All were reviewed by the medical monitor, Dr. Rivera, and none was assessed as related to study drug except SAE No. 2.

* **SAE No. 1** (placebo). Appendicitis on Day 43, appendectomy, recovered without sequelae. Not related.
* **SAE No. 2** (low dose). Drug-induced liver injury suspected on Day 57: ALT 6.2× ULN, bilirubin normal, i.e. Hy's law criteria were **not** met. Study drug was permanently discontinued and ALT normalised by Day 85. Assessed as *possibly related* by the investigator.
* **SAE No. 3** (high dose). Community-acquired pneumonia on Day 98, hospitalised for 4 days. Not related per the investigator; the sponsor's assessment is "unlikely related" given the timing.
* **SAE No. 4–7**: see the listings in the closed report (Appendix 2).

> **From the DSMB charter, section 7.2**
>
> The DSMB may recommend modification or termination of the study if the incidence of hepatic events meeting Hy's law criteria, or of grade 4 neutropenia, is judged to be substantially higher in either active arm than in the placebo arm.
>
> > In the absence of formal stopping boundaries for safety, such a judgement will take into account the totality of the data, e.g. the time course, reversibility and biological plausibility of a causal relationship.

Laboratory parameters
---------------------

Shifts from normal at baseline to grade ≥ 2 abnormalities were rare. Two participants in the high-dose arm had transient neutropenia (grade 2, absolute neutrophil count 1.0–1.5 × 10⁹/L) at Week 4, which resolved without dose interruption by Week 8. There were no cases of grade ≥ 3 neutropenia. Mean changes in lipids were small (LDL-C +0.12 mmol/L in the high-dose arm vs. −0.03 mmol/L on placebo) and are similar to those described for other drugs of the class, cf. Haddad et al. (2021).

Vital signs and ECG parameters showed no clinically meaningful changes. One participant (low dose) had a QTcF of 482 ms at Week 12, i.e. above the 480 ms threshold; the repeat ECG one hour later was 451 ms, and the participant continued treatment after review by the cardiologist, Dr. Weiss.

# Important protocol deviations

Important protocol deviations (n = 14) are listed below. Minor deviations are summarised in the closed report only.

1. Eligibility criteria not met (n = 3).
   - Two participants were randomised with a screening PASI of 11.5 and 11.8, below the required ≥ 12. Both were identified at the first monitoring visit. Per sponsor decision, they continued treatment.
   - One participant had a positive QuantiFERON test at screening that was misread as "indeterminate". Isoniazid prophylaxis was started on Day 22.
2. Dosing errors (n = 4), e.g. a missed dose at Week 8 due to a shipment delay at site No. 112 (Lyon). No participant received a higher dose than assigned.
3. Visits out of window (n = 6). Mostly over the Christmas holidays; none affected the primary endpoint assessment at Week 16.
4. Unblinding (n = 1). The site pharmacist at site No. 205 inadvertently opened an emergency unblinding envelope. Dr. Chen reviewed the case and confirmed that neither the treating investigator nor the participant was informed of the allocation.

\newpage

# Conclusions

No new safety signals were identified in this interim analysis. The overall incidence of TEAEs was similar across arms, the excess of injection-site reactions on active treatment is consistent with the phase I experience, and the single hepatic SAE did not meet Hy's law criteria. The study team therefore proposes that the DSMB recommend continuation of the study without modification.
The next interim review is planned at a data cut-off of 31 July 2024, or earlier if requested by the DSMB.

***

# Listings {-}

```{r listings, eval=params$show_listings}
adae |>
  filter(AESER == "Y") |>
  select(USUBJID, TRT01A, AEDECOD, ASTDY, AETOXGR, AEREL, AEOUT) |>
  arrange(TRT01A, USUBJID) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Listing 1. Serious adverse events (safety population)")
```

[^phase1]: Lindgren M, Okafor C, Barros J, et al. Safety and pharmacokinetics of ACM-4410 in healthy volunteers: a phase I, randomised, placebo-controlled study. *Br J Clin Pharmacol*. 2022;88(4):1712–1723.

[sap]: https://ctms.acme-pharma.example/studies/ACME-301/documents/SAP_v2.1_final_signed.pdf
